utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. I understand you have a submission to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And, indeed, it relates to two issues, one of which is very urgent, and it would need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first one is very brief. It relates to your decision on the site visit. I just want to mention that the Prosecution nominates Ms. Carolyn Edgerton as a replacement for Mr. Hogan. That's the first. And the second issue relates to our filing of an amended witness list and to clarify one matter, and I clarify it because of the response of Mr. Robinson. The filing relates to the replacement of Dr. Zecevic, and Dr. Zecevic was supposed to testify this week and the following week, so we nominated four witnesses to cover the hours that he was supposed to testify. The last two of these witnesses, Ms. Dzevlan and Mr. Mujkic, are not available this week, so I recall that Mr. Robinson made a response that the Defence could deal with Ms. Dzevlan, but Ms. Dzevlan is not able to travel this week. In relation to the other two witnesses that we have nominated for this week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who is another witness who is not available this week, in addition to Ms. Dzevlan?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ramiz Mujkic. That's number 147. He's the fourth on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Mr. Music, the Prosecution would like to have an early decision or remark of the Trial Chamber whether we can call him this week, because if we are allowed to call him, the witness would have to travel tomorrow morning to come here in time. So that's why we urgently need a decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to discuss that in private session, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, regarding Music?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He is not a protected witness. We could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We could go back to open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, we could go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from inquiry of that part, do you have any observation to make in response to the response of Mr. Robinson in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we have tried to find witnesses that are available on short notice when we became aware that Dr. Zecevic would not be available, and Mr. Hogan and Mr. Music are the only two that we could actually find to replace him on short notice. We are aware that there is a disclosure issue in relation to a statement of Mr. Music. We can definitely admit that this statement was not disclosed. We will argue why it was not done, but I can say it here also. It did not come up in a name search for the witness because the witness name could not be read on the first page. It was only now found in relation to other key words for which we were searching, and this is what I can say to this effect. I can also say that the statement does include new information, because the statement focused on another person in the chain of command that Mr. Music was actually dealing with, so -- on the Serb side. So that's why there is new information in there, but we would not -- we, the Prosecution, would not lead any information from that statement, because it's not relevant for our case, as we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is my understanding that Mr. Music appears in the February witness list, and, as such, it was notified to the Defence that he may come in February.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Indeed, all the witnesses that we have mentioned here are listed as one of the early -- now coming in February, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the case in the case of Mr. Hogan?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think he's the sixth or seventh next witness. And we have, on purpose, also nominated him. He is available, definitely, as he is here in The Hague. And in addition, he deals with issues that Dr. Karadzic is very familiar with, because he will deal with the locations and the topography of Sarajevo, basically, with one side issue, that he also took in materials from the Banja Luka archives. But the main topic of Mr. Hogan is basically the locations where incidents occurred and the visibility, what can be seen from where. So we thought that -- as Dr. Karadzic has addressed these topics very specifically with many witnesses, we thought that he would be able to deal with Mr. Hogan's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to reply, Mr. Robinson, on these issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We definitely recognise the difficulty that the Prosecution has in bringing witnesses on short notice, and undoubtedly we'll encounter those same difficulties in the course of our case. So we have that understanding that it's some need to be flexible. Practical problems that are, with respect to Mr. Music, we really haven't prepared any cross-examination of him at this point, even though he's on the list for February. In an ideal situation, we would be a month ahead, but I think that's completely unrealistic, given the volume of documents in this case and the amount of resources that we have. So we haven't really begun to really prepare, in all earnestness, his cross-examination. And we have a statement just disclosed to us only in B/C/S, I believe on Thursday or Friday. We intend to file tomorrow a disclosure violation motion based on the late disclosure of that statement and ask that the witness's testimony be excluded. If you follow your earlier pattern, you won't grant that motion, but you have in the past, in identical situations, required that the Prosecution delay for one, two, or even three months the calling of such witnesses, and so we don't think it would be fair, given that disclosure situation, to call Mr. Music in any event. With respect to Mr. Hogan, I suggest that we certainly hear his direct examination on Wednesday. We have no objection to doing that. It's supposed to take two hours. We can do our best to be prepared for his cross-examination on Thursday, and it's possible, given the nature of his testimony, that we can achieve that. On the other hand, if it turns out that there are other issues for him that would assist in the Defence case that we would like to ask him about, we may be disadvantaged by the late notice, and in such instance we could do our best to cross-examine him and try to ask that he be recalled, since he's in The Hague, for some other matters. But we're willing to do our best to accommodate the Prosecution's desire to call Mr. Hogan and have his testimony heard this week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter and give its ruling in the next session. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just seen information from the Office of the Prosecutor that we did not list Mr. Hogan as one of the early witnesses this month; indeed, not even this month. I'm just seeing this, that we had actually postponed him until we hear the last witnesses in the Sarajevo component of the case. So I was wrong in my understanding. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. He appears as the last one in the January and February list?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That said, let's draw the curtain and bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while this witness is brought in, perhaps we could profitably use the time to just alert you that, with respect to this particular witness, I'm going to have an objection to portions of his amalgamated statement that deal with unscheduled incidents. So I don't know if you want to take that up now or after he affirms his amalgamated statement and it's offered, but there's a number of unscheduled incidents that are described in the amalgamated statement and a number of associated exhibits that deal with unscheduled incidents, and we would be objecting to the admission of those portions of the statement and the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given our earlier decision, I don't think we have to repeat the rulings again. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that. But I think, given your earlier decisions, that would result in the exclusion of the associated exhibits. So you previously have been admitting the statement, but not admitting the associated exhibits dealing with unscheduled incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that when dealing with the associated exhibits. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gaynor. It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I understand you've previously testified in the trial of Stanislav Galic and in the trial of Dragomir Milosevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you've previously provided signed statements for this Tribunal, and you've provided information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You have reviewed an amalgamated statement containing relevant portions of your previous testimonies and of the information you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask that the first exhibit not be broadcast and that it be brought up. It's 22273, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, do you see a copy of the first page of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you also see a -- do you see your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to review that statement yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand there's one clarification you wish to make in respect of that statement and it concerns paragraph 85 of the statement. In your statement, Witness, you describe two air-bomb incidents, both of which took place at Safeta Hadzica Street. One of them was on the 26th of May, 1995, and the other was on the 28th of June, 1995. And in your statement, at paragraph 85, you say that you personally saw the modified air-bomb pass over the police station; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court whether you recall exactly whether that relates to the Safeta Hadzica Street incident of the 26th of May, 1995, or whether it refers to the incident at the same street of the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Now, after all this time, it's difficult to remember when exactly that happened, but it certainly happened in one of these two incidents. I believe I provided more accurate information in my first statement. I did not see it in either incident [as interpreted], but it was one of these two incidents. I was in the same place when these projectiles flew over, but whether it was the first case or the second case, I don't know. The bottom line is I saw that projectile only in one of the two incidents. And probably, since I gave statements several times, there may have occurred a misunderstanding about the date, whether I saw it in the first incident or the second incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer reads, in part, "I did not see it in either incident." Just to clarify the record, the position is you did see it in one of the two incidents, but you can't recall which one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right. I described in detail, in one of my statements, that I saw how that projectile flew over, but I cannot remember exactly now in which of the two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to that clarification, Mr. Witness, do you adopt that statement as your evidence, and would you provide the same answers if you were asked, under oath, about those topics today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that statement under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2163, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you planning to produce a public version of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can do, yes. We shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we give the number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2164.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I propose to read a brief summary of the statement that's just been admitted. The witness was a crime technician for the Centre for Public Security, CSB, in Sarajevo, of the Ministry of the Interior of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the RBiH MUP. He participated in investigations of shelling and sniping incidents occurring in Sarajevo between 1993 and 1995. The witness was involved in the investigation of a shelling incident in which three mortar rounds landed in the area of Alipasino Polje on 22nd January 1994. Six children were killed and five persons were wounded. The investigative team concluded that the origin of fire was from the west. That's Scheduled Incident G6. The witness also investigated a shelling incident on the 26th of May, 1995, in which a modified air-bomb struck a building near apartment blocks in Safeta Hadzica Street, destroying the top three floors of an apartment building. This explosion was followed by several artillery rounds. Two persons were seriously injured, and fifteen persons were slightly injured. The air-bomb was determined to have come from a west-south-west direction. That's Scheduled Incident G13. The witness also describes investigations of five unscheduled shelling incidents and three unscheduled sniping incidents. These incidents included an incident of the 18th of August, 1995, in which a bus of the Elektroprenos company, which was carrying civilians, was shot at, killing one girl and injuring fourteen other persons. That ends the summary, and I'll now begin the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us briefly what your role was while you worked for the RBiH MUP between 1993 and the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: My job, as a scenes-of-crime officer attached to the Security Services Centre, was to document evidence of a crime in question and, together with the rest of the investigating team, work on investigations. For certain cases, I took photographs, I sketched the crime scene and collected evidence that the crime really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In respect of shelling incidents, was it specifically your role to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, that was not my role, although I came to the same conclusions, based on the traces, as the rest of the team. That was more specifically the role of ballistics experts who were either on the scene, or a member of the so-called KDZ, the bomb squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, notwithstanding that it wasn't specifically your task to determine direction of fire, did you, in fact, receive training in crater analysis in order to determine direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes, I did undergo training, and I had ballistics experts as my teachers and instructors. Based on certain examinations on the scene, I learned, based on certain traces, to determine the direction of fire so I was able to come to a conclusion myself as to where the projectile had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions about cease-fires. I would like to know how, generally speaking, you became aware of the commencement of a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, we did not have any notice of cease-fires. It's just that I lived in that neighbourhood, where I lived and where I worked. So when there was no shelling, we took it that there was a cease-fire on, though cease-fires were interrupted by surprised shelling, of which, of course, we had not been warned. So if there was no shelling for a certain time, we called that "cease-fire." Otherwise, I absolutely didn't know whether there were any agreements as to whether there would or would not be shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that cease-fires were interrupted by surprised shelling. Could you clarify if this was typically how a cease-fire would come to an end, or were there occasions where you received warning about the end of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I never received such a warning. For me, a cease-fire was interrupted when I heard an explosion. And when such an explosion would occur, we all ran for shelter and waited for a while, until it became relatively quiet, in order to get out, which didn't mean that the shelling would not continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about extended periods of cease-fire which might go on for extended periods. Would you ever receive warning that an extended period of cease-fire was about to end?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand that you lived in Alipasino Polje for much of the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right, from 1992 until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to orient the Court to this part of Sarajevo, and I'd like to call up P1803. That can be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, while this is coming up, could you tell us a little bit about the background of Alipasino Polje? What kind of area is it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That is a strictly residential area. It has many high-rises. It was built in three stages, A, B and C. It is inhabited by several thousand civilian residents, and it was built in end 1970s, early 1980s, mostly for workers, blue-collar workers. It was a workers' neighbourhood, a civilian neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like the Registrar to bring up 65 ter 13564. I may have given the wrong P number for that, but that's the 65 ter number for it, please. This is page 11 of the Sarajevo-specific court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you take a pen, with the assistance of the Usher, and simply draw a circle around the area which you consider to constitute Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very good. We see the red marking which you have made around Alipasino Polje. Could you give the Court an idea of, approximately, the population of that area, to the best of your knowledge, during the period 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I think it was close to 10.000, because those are mostly high-rise buildings, a great number of residential units, and all these residential units were full. Some were even occupied by more than one family, because refugees had come to join their families and friends, just like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of any ABiH barracks in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Not that I know, there were no military installations there. It was a typically civilian neighbourhood, buildings occupied by civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you ever see ABiH artillery, or mortar units, or any ABiH heavy weapons of any description in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I did not see any. I lived in Alipasino Polje, C phase, and I can confirm that throughout that period I had not seen any weapons, absolutely no weapons, no heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like you to mark, for the Court, a number of locations referred to in your indictment [sic] -- excuse me, in your amalgamated statement. First of all, could you mark, with a "1," approximately the centre point of the three shells which landed on the 22nd of January, 1994, while the children were playing in the snow, according to your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just mark the figure "1" next to that, if you would.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you mark, with the number 2, the location of the school at Trg ZAVNOBiHa, referred to at page 7 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat what I've already said. The transcript says something different. It should say "Trg ZAVNOBiHa," and "ZAVNOBiH" has to be written in capital letters at that. That's right. Number 2, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 2 marks the location of the school where four were killed. Could you mark number 3 for Trg Rade Koncara, referred to at page 7 of your statement, where you say three were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Number 4, could you make Geteova Street 12, which was hit on the 22nd of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Number 5, could you mark Geteova Street 5, which was hit on the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: It's over here, where the green "6" is. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: With the number 6, could you mark the intersection of the two streets where the Elektroprenos bus was shot on the 18th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you put down the pseudonym "KDZ477" in the corner of the map somewhere, and today's date, which is January 31st.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that as a public document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to Incident G6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, for your information, the Court has already received documentation about this, and in that documentation it states -- and in your statement, it states that the direction of fire of the projectiles indicated that they were fired from the direction of Nedzarici. And I'd like you to clarify for the Court who determined the direction of fire of the projectiles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: The team consisted of the investigative judge, myself, the inspector from the Security Services, the inspector for Novi Grad, and ballistic experts. As for the direction of fire, it was the ballistics expert who was in charge of that. If he were not there, then the KDZ inspector and I were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the documentation which the Court has already received, it says that Mirza Sabljica and Borislav Stankov were present. Could you clarify what you understood their roles to be?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Those two gentlemen were ballistics experts, and that is to say that they were in charge of the type of grenade that we are talking about and where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They were in charge of what, exactly, in relation to the type of projectile?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Because they were experts for such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just clarify your earlier answer. It says "they were in charge of the type of grenade." That's what we are talking about, and where it came from. Just clarify, very briefly, what you meant.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Everybody on the team was in charge of a particular type of thing. I was in charge of taking photographs and carrying out certain measurements that the experts needed so that they could say what kind of shell it had to do with. That is to say that on the basis of the explosion, itself, it would be the investigative judge who would give them the authority to say what this was all about; what kind of explosion, what kind of shell, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, were the bodies of the victims still at the location when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, no, we went out later, when the entire team got together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what had become of the bodies of the victims before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, when such incidents occur, we are not the ones who would be out there on the spot, which is only natural, so a citizen who happened to be there would hope that somebody was still alive and then would take them, by car or in some other way, to the closest medical institution so that those persons could be assisted. If they're dead, they're dead, but perhaps the people who are transporting them were not even aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know if this incident took place during a cease-fire or not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, according to all my reports before that, and I was on duty at the time, for a number of days there hadn't been any shelling, so I know this was sudden. I think that the children went out to play in the snow because there hadn't been any shelling; not only there, but also in the broader area. Otherwise, they wouldn't have been outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to Incident G13, which you discuss at page 11 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up the next exhibit, and I ask that it not be broadcast. And it's 65 ter 16837, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document on the left-hand side of the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes. That is my report, and it's my signature, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this report, you state that a high-impact projectile came from aggressors' positions to the west, shelling the Pavle Goranin suburb. Later on, you say that besides that projectile, 10 more shells of undetermined calibre landed at the same location. First of all, who determined the direction of fire at this incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In this specific incident, I don't know who it was that determined it. I think that it is contained in other reports. However, on the basis of the traces left by the projectiles, I mean those 10 projectiles, in that residential area, it was established that it had come from the west, and this is one of the two incidents where I actually saw the projectile that was flying from the western side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How did you know that 10 other shells of undetermined calibre had arrived?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Those shells exploded in the immediate vicinity of the police building where I was. That is to say that I could hear the explosions, themselves, very well. Afterwards, when I went out to the scene, and when I actually saw where the explosion had taken place, I saw that these were 10 shells of an unidentified calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that it would not be that difficult for you to produce a public version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit those two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original document will be Exhibit P2166, under seal, and the public version will be Exhibit P2167.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I now call up, and this can be broadcast, 65 ter 21214.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about the area of Sarajevo that you've just talked about, the Pavle Goranin area. Now, if you could take your pen and draw a circle around the Pavle Goranin area, and just write "PG."

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I understand your police station, where you worked, is also visible. Could you identify that and mark "MUP"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]. Yes, that's the building where you can just see the red roof, and it's at the very beginning there, or, rather, on the western side of this settlement, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, is it right that part of Alipasino Polje is also visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right. That is to say, between Alipasino Polje and this neighbourhood, there is a parking-lot. Alipasino Polje are these tall buildings on the western side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just put "AP" over the buildings you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it right that Alipasino Polje continues to the left side of the photograph and it's not all visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right. We just see part of the C phase here and a part of A phase, but part of B phase cannot be seen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you mark Safeta Hadzica Street with "SH"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That street cannot be seen here for the buildings, but I can mark where it is actually located. [Marks]. It runs throughout this photograph from the west to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the 10 shells that you just described a moment ago. Could you give the Court a picture of where the 10 shells landed and where the modified air-bomb landed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Shells were falling from this building next-door to the police building - that's the northern side - and then one, two, three, four, five, these buildings here, this area that is circled [indicated]. And where I marked this building "PG," that's where the modified bomb fell on the roof of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best if you just put small dots where the 10 artillery shells landed, approximately speaking.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Some of them hit the building. I cannot remember exactly, but from where it says "MUP" all the way to this last building here [indicates]. So it's this row of buildings in the Pavle Goranin neighbourhood, so they did not go in depth. It was these exposed buildings from the MUP to Majdanska Street that goes down towards this TV station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So, in summary, is it fair to say that the 10 shells -- the 10 artillery shells landed over a broad expanse of the Pavle Goranin area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, it's about 100 to 150 metres long. As you can see in this photograph, these buildings are close to each other, and they went down all the way to Majdanska. Up to 200 metres, maximum. We cannot really see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask it this way: On the basis of the distribution of the shells, did they appear to be aiming at one specific location in Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Apart from civilian buildings or perhaps the police station, there was nothing specific to be targeted there except for what had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of any ABiH barracks in Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of any ABiH mortars, artillery, or tanks, or any heavy weaponry of any kind in Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I probably would have heard firing if there were such things there, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your police station, approximately how many officers were employed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, but perhaps, including all the technical staff, the Crime Prevention police and the police, perhaps about 100 people in all shifts, I think. I'm not sure, because my centre was actually in town, so I was detached there. In order to be exposed to less risk, we were working at police stations that were closer to the places where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were the police officers armed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Every policeman was armed either with a pistol or -- actually, I think that uniformed policemen at the time had rifles as well, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Generally speaking, could you describe the nature of the population in Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: It's a civilian neighbourhood, blue-collar, most of it built before Alipasino Polje. Families lived as they did in all other neighbourhoods in town. I didn't really know who lived there, but when I worked on break-and-entry cases, I saw that these were ordinary citizens, blue-collar workers who were employed there or elsewhere. So it wasn't a military neighbourhood, as some were in town. This was a purely civilian neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And your answer refers to the period 1993 until the end of the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for D533, please. Sorry, I should have sought the admission of that. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you sign the very bottom, in the white area, your pseudonym, which is "KDZ477," and write down today's date?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I'd like to tender that as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could have D533, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, given that we are sitting for a shorter period of time today, we are minded to have two 20-minute breaks today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the first break will be at 20 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's perfect. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document in front of you, I think, Witness, is a photo file which you prepared in respect of this incident. Is that correct? That's Incident G13.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Correct. That is the first photograph of my photo documentation prepared for the case that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The photograph that we see in front of us doesn't show a tremendous amount of destruction, I think it's fair to say. Could you explain why you took it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: This photograph shows a yard in Safeta Hadzica 102. It is the backyard. One of these projectiles fell there. I went there just for the sake of the record, to see in which area these shells fell; not because of the damage caused by the projectile, but simply so that we would see what the sequence of events was as it occurred at the time. You see this wall here [indicates]. These are garages of the police station that can be seen behind with the red roof. You can barely see the arrow, though. I marked it at a later stage, once I had pasted the photograph here, and it shows exactly where the projectile fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is the arrow intended to depict the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, no, it is not there to prove any kind of direction of fire. It just shows the place where it exploded. I could have put an arrow there from anywhere just to show where the explosion took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look at photo 5, the fifth page of this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain what this is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In this photograph, we can see the damage caused by the explosion of the projectile on the western side of the building in Safeta Hadzica number 2 between the third and fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is this one of the 10 shells that you referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right, this is one of the 10 shells. Underneath the photograph, it says "the third projectile." However, not necessarily, because we went from one point of explosion to another and then we compiled our own record, as in 1, 2 and 3, and we called this one the third projectile, although it does not necessarily have to mean that that is the exact sequence in which they actually exploded. Perhaps it was the seventh one or the tenth one. I had no way of telling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: From what direction had this projectile travelled prior to impact?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Since this is the western side of the building, that is to say it came from the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we have photo 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this photograph, we see an arrow and a dotted line. Could you explain what the arrow and the dotted line mean?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: This is a photograph that I took. The damage that can be seen on this photograph was caused by one of these 10 projectiles. Number 8 marks the first place, the first point of impact of this shell. The shell continued along this interrupted line that I marked later on, the dotted line, and it hit the western part of the house in the photograph. And now the arrow and the dotted line show exactly, on the basis of these two points, the direction from which the projectile came from. You can see that very nicely here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just, finally, Mr. Witness, could I ask you a few questions about the start of the war, when you and your family were living in Dobrinja. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe the circumstances in which you left Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In April 1992, I lived in Dobrinja 4, in an apartment, with my parents and sister. Just before the conflict, without any reason whatsoever, there was gun-fire fired at my neighbourhood. I claim, with full responsibility, that there was nothing behind the apartment building where I lived, and my apartment was hit several times. One day, I don't know which date it was and I don't really want to remember that at all, I saw a group of armed people walking across a lawn that could be seen from my apartment. They walked into our entranceway, and there was a lot of panic there because people had no idea why there was gun-fire. My parents told me that they went up to the fourth floor to stay with our friends, neighbours, who were of Serb ethnicity. Armed soldiers - they were armed with rifles and some even had grenades on their vests - asked for my ID. Inter alia, when they read my name, they singled me out. I didn't know why. Later on, I think it was just because my name is what it is. I don't know. Later on, I realised that one of their men was injured somehow. But they didn't take me when they left, but my parents said that I had to leave the apartment. I left. I crossed the Mojmilo Hill and I went to Alipasino Naselje to stay with a relative. There was shelling further on, but I went back to Alipasino Polje, I found my relative, and I stayed with him at his apartment. Later on, without any kind of agreement having been reached previously, but it seemed that way, it just so happened that my parents came as well. So we met up there in Alipasino Polje and stayed there from 1992 until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the group of armed people who you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I assumed that they were ethnic Serbs, because on their uniforms they had insignia of the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And were you free to return to your house after that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No. From then, all the way up to 1996, we could not return, in order for my father to get the apartment in 1996 or 1997, and later on he exchanged that apartment for another apartment in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That ends the examination-in-chief, Mr. President. Perhaps I can address now the associated exhibits. I believe that Your Honours have previously indicated that you do not wish to receive supporting documentation for unscheduled shelling and sniping incidents. And if that is the case, we won't tender any of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, I think that has been the case. As far as I remember, it has been the Chamber's ruling that while we allow the Prosecution to lead evidence going to the specific incidents which are not listed in the indictment or its schedules, on the ground that it may go to establishing the necessary general requirements for crimes against humanity or to the elements of some of the underlying offences. However, we find it not very helpful to admit detailed evidence regarding those incidents because we are not ultimately making beyond-reasonable-doubt findings as to those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. President, in that case, the two scheduled incidents which are dealt with in this statement are G6 and G13, and all of the documents relating to those incidents are already in evidence. So I won't tender any other exhibit at all. I can provide the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we identify one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the first thing which can be admitted is 09604.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. That's P1696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my list, P1696 was listed as 65 ter 09605. I refer to 09604, a MUP report on 22nd January 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll just consult Mr. Reid for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- regarding the shelling in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that case, I'd like to tender 09604, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that will be admitted. Let's give it a number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P2169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the next one seems to be -- I think we dealt with everything. The next one is 16837, but we admitted it during the course of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've dealt with everything, Mr. President. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break. This time, we're going to have a break for 25 minutes. The Chamber will have a consultation or deliberation. So we'll resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, considering the time estimate for the examination-in-chief of the next witness and the time allotted for the cross-examination of this witness and the next witness, it seems to the Chamber -- it seems likely to the Chamber that the evidence of the next witness will be concluded only in the middle of Wednesday, leaving only about a session, i.e., about an hour and a half, for another witness. So, therefore, as suggested by Mr. Robinson, we decided to hear the examination-in-chief of Mr. Hogan on Wednesday, which may continue on Thursday a bit. Then we expect Mr. Karadzic to conduct his cross-examination of Mr. Hogan, and I think that will be it for this week. Therefore, I would advise you not to make arrangements to call Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And taking this opportunity, Mr. Robinson, having received, from General Van Baal's submission, his diary, I wonder whether you are minded to withdraw your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we withdraw that motion at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We note that withdrawn. Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. In your amalgamated statement, in para 3, you said that your position was that of a forensic technician?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: We call it "crime technician," "crime scene technician."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You joined the police in January 1993. From January to October or November, when you moved to the Crime Service, did you go to the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which police officers did go?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come that you didn't?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, I was not in that category that went to the front-lines. I believe the uniformed policemen did stints on the front-line, but I don't know who or how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you started working on criminal investigations as a scenes-of-crimes officer from November 1993, and you worked on cases of theft, breaking and entering, murder, and other serious crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes. I investigated all serious crimes that were within the purview of the Crime Scenes Service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving the witness in my head-set, but fortunately he's speaking loud enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your findings always end up before the court?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I did my part of the job, and it was sent by post to the specific police station which was in charge of specific crimes. Now, whether those police stations sent my findings on to the courts, I don't know. That's up to them. My job was to do my part of the work and, by official post, to send my reports to the competent police station, which would then forward them, or not, perhaps, to the courts. It was not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to the procedure that would be sent to the Prosecutor's office that brings an indictment. Have you ever testified before Bosnian courts about your reports in the cases on which you worked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In the 18 years that I've been working as a policeman, there were only two such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. In any case, it was after the war, where I once testified concerning a murder, and once a burglary/theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you have never testified before about incidents from the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, this is the first -- this is the only place where I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 26 of today's transcript, you said that when the soldiers approached, your parents told you to go to your Serb friend who lived on the fourth floor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they go too? Why only you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Who, the parents or I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't your parents also go to the fourth floor to find shelter? Why only you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't know. Parents -- like parents, they sent only me, and they stayed on the ground floor, where our apartment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these people checked ID papers and took some people aside and did not single out others?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I know that they checked the ID papers of our Serb neighbours, and mine, too. And I believe on the same floor there was another Serb family, but only I was taken to one side. I don't know what happened on the floors above and below. And at that moment, by the way, I didn't even know what was going on with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your parents later tell you what happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Exactly as I said. Since only my apartment was on the ground floor, there were no other apartments there, my parents had to stand outside their apartment, on their own landing, and there was one armed soldier on the ground floor. The other soldiers, I don't know exactly how many of them, took the stairs to go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described to us that they were looking for someone in specific; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't know what they were up to and what they intended, but they took me to one side, only me, out of the five people on the floor. Whether they were looking for someone in specific or what their intentions were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your father wasn't taken away, was he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Nobody was taken away at that time, because they left the building for other reasons and they went back the same way they came from. There was no abuse at that time, apart from the mental stress, against me or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 14 of your amalgamated statement, you say - sorry, paragraph 15 - that you worked on 350 different cases, and 52 of them were related to genocide. Who determined that these cases related to genocide, and how was that defined?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: The cases that I marked as such, those 52, concern investigations of sniping, gun-fire, shelling, and the use of modified air-bombs. In my service, my superiors said -- qualified these cases as relating to genocide. There was one department inside the Security Services Centre that was in charge of all cases related to genocide. They handled all these cases, and through them such cases were later forwarded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So anything that happened during the combat operations was classified as genocide?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You later explained that within those 52 investigations, the number of cases was actually smaller, because sometimes there would be a number of investigations relating to one-and-the-same case for various reasons, because victims were found subsequently, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In those investigations, there were certain shelling incidents where there were no human casualties, only material damage, but I went out on each such case and did my work, like in every other case that is before this Court, and they are also entered in my diary that I kept in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there were 52 investigations, but not as many cases; there were repeated investigations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, there were no repeated investigations. Those are 52 investigations, 52 visits of a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times did you act as a ballistics man in those 52 cases?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it help you to see your reports to see in which cases the ballistics expert was missing and you determined the ballistics elements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: The investigating judge should have been present in each investigation, making minutes and indicating how many members of the team there were. If there was no ballistics expert and no member of the KDZ, then I would, based on the evidence, determine the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times was the investigating judge not there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In those cases where I worked, the investigating judge would not come to the scene when there were no human victims and there were no elements of serious incident as determined by the judge, himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 15 November 1995, on page 3 you say that after all these years, you had acquired a certain experience, so you conducted investigations routinely. And you say: "When I say 'routinely,' I mean to say that as time went on and I gained more experience, the accuracy of investigations improved, and I started going out to crime scenes on my own. I had received enough training and experience to be able to determine what each trace meant." That was November 1995. What point in time would you say marks the beginning of your independence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Before I started working as a scenes-of-crime officer, I received high-quality training in the Security Services Centre, itself, and my instructors were ballistics experts. They taught me well to handle investigations of crime scenes. As shellings became more frequent, by coming out to the scene and looking at photographs taken by other colleagues, and with continuing education from other ballistics experts, I can say that it was not difficult to master the investigation of a scene of explosion and to learn to determine where the projectile came from, what kind of damage it created. On the scene, I would learn how to photograph a scene from up close, from a distance, to observe significant details. And when I said "routinely," that means all that I have described. I don't mean "routinely" in the sense of hastily. That would imply mistakes made in a rush. It means an approach informed by experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say on the same page that the local police was supposed to secure the crime scene, but in some cases, it was very difficult due to continuous shelling, and sometimes, even during the on-site investigation, itself, another shell would come. Could you name a few examples?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but during an investigation I was doing, a modified air-bomb exploded on the radio/television building. There was an investigating judge there and officers from the CSB. And another day, I don't know if there was an explosion of a modified air-bomb in the Geteova Street or was it the radio/television building first, but we did those two investigations on the same day. When we came to the Geteova Street number 5, a certain number of shells had fallen on Alipasino Polje neighbourhood, Stage A, and you could still see the smoke after the explosion. I was under so much stress that day that I worked under sedatives that day to be able to work normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that incident. You say on the same page that in cases when there was more than a certain number of wounded and dead, the wounded would usually have been taken away, removed, "... even before we arrived. We had to rely on blood-stains and witness statements to determine the position of the body." Is this the same procedure you followed in investigating murders?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In which period, in which murders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You worked, as you said, on homicide investigations. Did you proceed the same way on homicide investigations, without a body in place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I can't remember all the murder investigations I did, but there were cases when the body was still there and there were investigations when the body was not there. Now, of course, when a thing like that happens, human life is the highest priority. Before I arrived, somebody must have administered first aid, either medical personnel or passersby, and they would have first taken the person to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say: "We would collect fragments of projectiles on the spot, but this job was soon taken over by members of the KDZ, and these fragments were sent to ballistics experts to determine the type of projectile." Did ballistics experts really determine the type of projectiles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: If the reports are there, then they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Weren't ballistics experts supposed to determine something else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't know. It's the job of ballistics experts. I believe it was also their job to determine the type of round, the type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you say: "We also made measurements in order to be able to produce a map of the area." In a previous statement, you said "sketch" -- sorry, you said "map," and then you changed that to "sketch." Also, in the statement of 15 November, you said "map," and then you changed it to "sketch." But you say: "In some cases we could not do that because of the heavy shelling, and taking measurements takes a lot of time." Do you believe that an investigation without measurements is valid?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems the transcript is not quite correct: [In English] "In previous statements, you said "sketch" -- sorry, you said "map." [Interpretation] No, you said "plan," and then you changed that to "sketch." [In English] "In some cases, we couldn't do it -- we didn't do it -- we couldn't do it because of the shelling, because the measurement --"

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I had no interpretation just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He read in English, and you didn't get the interpretation. Mr. Karadzic, try to read out your statement again. So what is your question? Where were we, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4 of the 1995 statement. It says: "We also made measurements in order to be able to produce the map of the area. In some cases, we were unable to do that because of the heavy shelling, because taking measurements takes a long time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you then conclude that investigation if you had no measurements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I've already said that I was supposed to take photographs, to make a drawing, not a plan, of the crime scene, and in some cases I would do that as the investigating judge instructed. He decided whether I should make a drawing or not. I was not alone in that team that investigated. There were also other people, and their names are indicated in the crime scene investigation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I understood correctly, you made sketches.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In some investigations, I did, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who would have made a sketch in those cases when there were no measurements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I believe in some cases, the ballistics expert made a sketch that he needed for his own expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did he make a sketch if he had no measurements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: There were no measurements that I made, but he probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But a sketch indicates all spatial relations, distances. How can you make a sketch without measurements? You are supposed to take measurements, not the ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In some cases, the ballistics experts did. I believe the ballistics man did the sketch and the measurements in the case of the 22nd January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same page 4, last paragraph, you say: "I am familiar with the fundamental elements of ballistics, enough to determine the type of weapon and the direction of fire. Further analysis is the work of a ballistics expert. With experience, we all became experts. Sometimes I would be able to determine nearly the precise place where the projectile was fired, as well as its trajectory, especially when it landed at an angle of almost 90 degrees." Well, the first question is: On the 22nd January, Mr. Sabljica testified here and said that he only gave instructions, what kind of measurements should be taken, and that the scenes-of-crime officer did the measurements; he didn't. Did you participate in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In some cases, I make the photographs. I'm not sure, but if you show me my report, I think it will say photographs were taken, but I didn't take the measurements. As for what he said, it's fine. After all this time, maybe he got it wrong. I would like to see the report of the ballistics expert, because it should also indicate whether he made measurements or not. My photo file alone is not the whole case file. The case file contains all the witness statements, and the reports of the inspectors, the report of the ballistic expert, as well as my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take into account that I have to wait for interpretation. That's why I'm making this pause. Now, here is the question: Is it true, what it says here, that you knew the basics of ballistics science, that with experience you all became experts, and sometimes you were perfectly able to determine the exact place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: All I can say is that I was able to distinguish a mortar shell from a gun shell, from a rifle round, a pistol round, et cetera. When I see the tail-fin of a mortar shell, I was able to say that it was a mortar shell, not a gun shell. Those are the basics, to be able to distinguish heavy weaponry from lighter weaponry. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, you say that when a shell would fall into a river, it would be difficult to establish the direction. Is it difficult or impossible, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a ballistics expert. It was impossible for me, but perhaps it was possible for a ballistics expert. It was impossible for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the next -- third paragraph on that page, you say: "It was not our task to establish the exact place where the projectile had been fired from. Other experts dealt with the origin, and I can ascertain the position where fire was opened. They dealt with the characteristics of the projectile ..." Et cetera, et cetera. In every one of your investigations, did you have these experts who would actually establish that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember a case where you certainly did have this kind of an expert; you established the direction and he establishes the distance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: For example, there was a ballistics expert with me on the 22nd of January, 1994; two of them, as a matter of fact. And they were doing it, or they would send it to their colleagues who were of the same profession. I really don't know what their findings said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says that they established the distance -- or, rather, the direction, and that they were never in a position to establish the distance. That's what they say. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I did not. All of these findings of ballistics experts did not reach me, actually. Together with all the documents that were compiled, they were sent probably to the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your amalgamated statement, you say, in paragraph 28, that as crime technicians, you had to attend autopsies, take photos of the autopsy involved. You say: "It is also during the autopsy that an expert determines the exact canal between the entry and exit wound. We have to write down all the relevant information the expert finds during the autopsy." Did you attend these autopsies?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Yes, the job of a crime technician is to attend autopsies. That is done to this day, except that in war, I was not present during all autopsies in the case of all the victims in the cases that I dealt with. During some of these examinations of corpses in mortuaries, perhaps there were some of my colleagues who were closer to the mortuary concerned, because the police is closer to the hospital and the superior officers agreed that a forensic doctor would carry out the post-mortem and a different crime technician could do his job, so that we would not be exposed to additional risks in a]the time of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there really a risk in an autopsy room? What, if any?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, not in the room, itself, but the risk is en route. I could be in a shelled area as I would be coming to the autopsy room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "We have to attend ..." I'm quoting you verbatim. So we would have to expect these autopsy findings in every case, and that would include photographs and also a described trajectory of the projectile through the body, itself, the canal that you're referring to. Witness, does that exist in all of your investigations? That would be of great assistance to us. Can you indicate where it actually is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't have that. Now, who decides on these autopsies? Just like for on-site investigations, we received information from the duty officer, and then a forensic officer would ask for a crime technician to take photographs of the autopsy, itself. In cases when an autopsy was not carried out, only photographs were taken of corpses in the mortuary, that is. Now, as for attending all of these post-mortems, I don't know whether that kind of thing was scheduled, whether it was done all the time, and whether there are such findings or not, because I was not really in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did attend autopsies, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I do not remember specifically which ones I did attend. There were a few autopsies -- or, rather -- well, yes, there were a few autopsies that were carried out at the morgue in Dobrinja. I don't know exactly in which cases. To this day, my job is to attend autopsies when the forensic doctor asks me to attend, and he does so on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would your diary be of assistance? Do you have such entries in your diary?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: I don't think that I recorded that kind of attendance in my diary, because if I were to attend an autopsy, I wouldn't really write that down in my diary as something special. I only recorded visits to scenes, but not autopsies that were related to those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these proper autopsies or was it -- excuse me for using this kind of language, but sort of autopsies that were slapped together?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, you cannot really say it was just slapped together. Although it was wartime, we tried to do our work properly, and to do the technical things as they should be done, and to record all of it. Now, I'm not competent to speak on behalf of a forensic pathologist or doctor. I cannot say that he would slap that kind of thing together. First of all, I'm too well brought up for that kind of thing, and, secondly, I wouldn't like to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not saying anything. I would just like us to establish how long a proper autopsy takes, how much time, an autopsy that you would attend, one that would be admissible before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, that really has to do with forensic medicine again, and I'm not competent to speak about that, how long it should take. I attended autopsies that lasted longer than half an hour, an hour, and so on. It is really a forensic doctor who should say when an autopsy is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So then we can say that your experience with autopsies ranges between half an hour and an hour?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: No, some lasted even three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 30, you say that a modified air-bomb does not fall apart into too much shrapnel. What is your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: As opposed to mortar shells that are made to kill personnel, so it falls apart into thousands of pieces. This was the first time in my life that I came across this kind of thing, modified air-bombs. I did not find the kind of shrapnel left by a mortar shell. Concrete walls were torn apart by these modified air-bombs, but the traces, if I can put it that way, were not the same like in the case of a mortar shell, where there are thousands of particles involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you gather any fragments of this modified air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: In most cases, as far as modified air-bombs are concerned, I took photographs, again, in accordance with the technical capabilities I had. As for the on-site investigations, ballistics experts were there, and on the very spot they would take these -- collect these fragments and take them away for further analysis. The entire team worked together on collecting all of this evidence, but at the explosion site, itself, we would find what we would find on the tarmac, but I did not take any of this, because what had been agreed upon was that the ballistics experts would take these particles to the MUP, to the Centre of the Security Services, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are obviously familiar with the fact that an air-bomb has to collide head on with an obstacle in order to explode. And then you mentioned that ricochet in the same paragraph. You first said that in your transcript in the Milosevic case 1909 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in your statement on the 12th of February this year [as interpreted], you say what you mean by ricochet, and you say: "By 'ricochet,' I mean that if the bomb hit various surfaces before coming to its final resting place, we would be able, by examining --" I'm doing a sight translation from the English: "Examining the impact points to establish the path of the projectile." How many ricochet bombs did you investigate and how many such places did you see?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: As far as this is concerned, like in the case of all other projectiles, the projectile has a contact with a surface before it explodes, and then there is that ricochet trace. I remember that I was working on an investigation at the RTV centre, and then part of this bomb, some part of that projectile, left a trace on the roof before it actually exploded at the point of explosion at the RTV centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Do you know, roughly, what the velocity is of a modified air-bomb? It flies at which speed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert to establish its exact speed. However, at the moment when I would see it flying over the police building -- well, I'm not saying that it's exactly above the police building, but near the police building. It was visible, at any rate, as opposed to rifle shots that cannot be seen. This could be seen. However, I am not competent to say what its speed was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, you say, in 34, that a mortar can be adjusted that the shell lands in an area that is normally about 10 square metres large. When you use a modified air-bomb, such precise targeting is not possible. And then further on, you say that it means that they weren't serially produced. What about these engines? Were they improvised, or were they manufactured in a factory, and did they have proper plates and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: These were rocket-launchers. If we are talking about air-bombs, they are ejected from aircraft. And at the top of this rocket-launcher, there would be these bombs as well, and then we would call them modified air-bombs. As opposed to mortar and rifle barrels, these were launched from a different place. According to what the ballistics expert says, they were not fired from artillery pieces, but from certain ramps that could be adjusted, going higher up or lower down, or left or right. However, it was not the kind of precision that one has in case of mortars and guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have quite a bit of experience in ballistics, do you agree that all rockets are fired from rocket-launchers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Well, probably from certain launchers. Again, as I said, this is what ballistics experts said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these engines were engines that originally had a different kind of warhead, but that they were manufactured in a factory, that they had their plates and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ477
utterances.text: Probably. I saw these engines at different scenes. In a particular -- in the case of a particular incident in Geteova Street number 4, they were found in this building, the four barrels, and the ballistics experts took them away. So I saw these rockets. I did not write that down, though. I agree that most probably they were manufactured in a factory and had serial numbers. However -- they would have to be found by ballistics experts in case they were not destroyed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
